title: Truth Tables, Tautology and Contradiction
quickIdea: A truth table lists every interpretation. If every row is true the formula is a tautology, if every row is false it is a contradiction, and anything else is a contingency.
remember: A formula with n variables has 2^n rows: 4 for two variables, 8 for three.
Tautology: true in every row. Contradiction: false in every row. Contingency (satisfiable and falsifiable): true in some rows and false in others.
There are 2^(2^n) distinct truth functions of n variables: 16 of two variables, 256 of three.
To prove a tautology, every row must be true - one falsifying row is enough to disprove it.
Two formulas are equivalent exactly when they have identical columns, so one truth table settles an equivalence question.
Column order: build innermost brackets first, then work outwards.

example.prompt: Is (not p and (p or q)) -> q a tautology?
example.work: not p and (p or q) simplifies to not p and q. Then (not p and q) -> q is equivalent to p or not q or q, which is true regardless of p and q.
example.answer: Yes, a tautology. Both rows that could falsify it fail: the antecedent is true only when p is false and q is true, and there q is true.

gateAngle: GATE 2021 Set 1 Q.7 gives two formulas and asks which is a tautology: S1 = (not p and (p or q)) -> q is one, S2 = q -> (not p and (p or q)) is not, because it fails at p = q = true. The exam wants the falsifying row, not a full table.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many rows does the truth table of a formula in p, q, r, s have, and how many distinct truth functions of three variables exist?
variations.why: Rows = 2^4 = 16. Truth functions of n variables = 2^(2^n), so for n = 3 that is 2^8 = 256.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Is (p -> q) or (q -> p) a tautology?
variations.why: If p is false then p -> q is true. If p is true then q -> p is q -> true, which is true. So one disjunct is always true, and a disjunction with a true disjunct is true.

trap.what: Treating implication as 'both sides equal', or assuming a formula is a tautology because it looks balanced.
trap.why: Implication is false in exactly one row: antecedent true and consequent false. Every other row is true, including rows where the antecedent is false.
trap.counterexample: q -> (not p and (p or q)) looks like the tautology above but is false at p = true, q = true: the right side becomes (false and true) = false, so true -> false = false.

check.question: A formula in three variables is false in exactly one row. Is it a tautology, a contradiction, or a contingency?
check.explanation: Seven of the eight rows are true and one is false, so it is neither always true nor always false.
